title: Imitating the useful qualities of irrational animals
english: Have we not taught you explicitly to take unhesitating eagerness from the ant, and craftsmanship from the bee? For it is possible, as I said before, to pluck certain excellent qualities even from the irrational animals that suit a rational condition—yet these things are said for our shame and reproach. Since you did not imitate God, Scripture says, imitate the ant. Have you never seen a true father rebuking his children, and after much instruction leading them to imitate the household servants, saying openly: “Imitate even the servant, who is lower in rank but superior in skill”? So the God who loves humanity, to expose our ingratitude, brings forward the ant to convict our hesitation, and the bee to convict our laziness. And it is clear from these things that nothing evil was made by God; rather, he gave you perception and a discerning mind, to flee the habits of the irrational animals and to seize their excellent qualities. For the lion can also be an image of virtue, when you take the image not as tyranny but as courage—for tyranny is one thing, and courage another. Therefore Scripture, announcing the Savior who was to rise from Judah, says: “Judah is a lion’s cub; from the shoot, my son, you went up; crouching down, you slept like a lion, and like a cub” (Genesis 49:9). See how great a likeness the divine word constructs from the excellent qualities found in the irrational animals. It is possible, then, to imitate the lion with understanding; and it is possible also to imitate the serpent, not in injecting venom, but in taking on understanding—just as the Savior says to the apostles: “Be prudent as the serpent” (Matthew 10:16). Therefore, if the creature were worthless, he would not call his own image to imitate what is worthless, saying, “Be prudent as the serpent.” Imitate not the serpent’s venom, not its rage, but its understanding. For if you imitate its venom, David cries out against you in accusation, saying: “Their rage is like the likeness of the serpent” (Psalm 58:4). But if you imitate its understanding, you become a disciple of Christ, the one who said: “Be prudent as the serpent” (Matthew 10:16). For since the serpent is more prudent than all the wild beasts, as was just read, he set prudence against prudence—not so that you may learn to devise deceit, but so that you may learn to avoid deceit. For the God who loves humanity wants us to be not evildoers but prudent persons; and the prudent person is one thing, the evildoer another. The prudent person, then, is prudent not for practicing evil but for fleeing evil; he uses prudence not for weaving plots against others, but for escaping the plots woven by others. The evildoer, however, is the murderer, the deceiver, the one who contrives evils for others. Such a prudent man was Jacob—prudent as the serpent, not venomous as the serpent.

title: One animal image, many meanings
english: For when he was about to meet his brother Esau, who was full of malice and murderous intent, he entreated God, saying, “Lord, rescue me from my brother Esau, for I am very afraid of him” (Genesis 32:11). He begged God, offering his prayer as against an evil man. But when he met his brother, he softened his anger with courtesy and flattery, and quenched his wickedness. What does he say to Esau? “I have seen your face as one sees the face of God” (Genesis 33:10). If Jacob said this to defeat his brother through deceit, he spoke wrongly; but if he said it to escape fear, he used prudence well. So be prudent as the serpent—not hot-tempered, not venomous, but prudent, and innocent as doves (Matthew 10:16).

Now the dove can be taken as an image of either vice or virtue. Hear how. If you are thoughtless and undiscerning, and acquainted only with evil, Scripture accuses you as senseless. For it says, “Ephraim is like a senseless dove, without a heart” (Hosea 7:11). If, then, you flee thoughtlessness and achieve innocence, you have perfect understanding, not mixing it with evil. And you hear from the Lord, “Be prudent as serpents and innocent as doves” (Matthew 10:16).

So do not read the Scriptures carelessly, brother, and do not take the images from them as images of vice, when Scripture assigns one meaning to one thing and another meaning to another. Do you want to learn? Pay close attention to what is said. Scripture speaks of a lion: “Judah is a lion’s cub; from the shoot, my son, you went up; lying down, you slept like a lion” (Genesis 49:9). Here “like a lion” signifies courage. For it also applies the same image to the righteous person: “The righteous person is confident like a lion” (Proverbs 28:1). The righteous person, then, is courageous—not in doing evil, but in despising the attacks brought by the wicked.

Scripture also calls the Savior a lion, because he is from a royal tribe. For just as the lion is king of the four-footed animals, so the tribe of Judah ruled over the Jews, and from it the Savior arose. And do not think, beloved, that it is unworthy of Christ to be compared to the image of a lion. For Scripture shapes this image even for the Godhead itself. Hear what the prophet says: “A lion will roar—who will not fear? The Lord God has spoken—who will not prophesy?” (Amos 3:8). So Christ is compared to a lion for power, for fearsomeness, and for royalty.

The devil is also called a lion—not as powerful, nor as fearsome, but as a striker, as a tyrant, as a destroyer. The blessed apostle Peter says about him: “Behold, your enemy the devil prowls around like a lion, seeking someone to devour” (1 Peter 5:8). Distinguish, then, the meanings of the readings, lest things that seem contradictory in the wording confuse your mind. Scripture said “lion” and “lion”—but one according to what is royal and powerful, the other according to what is destructive and deadly.

title: The same image for righteous and wicked and the honey of the divine words
english: Scripture portrays both the righteous and the ungodly by means of one image. It says, “The righteous will flourish like a palm tree, and will be multiplied like a cedar in Lebanon” (Psalm 92:12). It first drew the image of the righteous, and then in the same way the image of the ungodly. For it says, “I saw the ungodly exalted and lifting himself up like the cedars of Lebanon” (Psalm 37:35).

See how it has produced the same image but divided the meanings by its wording. For the ungodly it says, “I saw the ungodly exalted and lifting himself up like the cedars,” while for the righteous it did not say, “He will bloom like a cedar in Lebanon,” but, “He will be multiplied.” So imitate the bee, fellow human, as Scripture itself teaches us to imitate with respect to diligence. Scripture says, “Go to the bee and learn how industrious she is” (Proverbs 6:8).

Learn not that she has a sting, but that she produces honey. If you copy the sting of the bee, David accuses you when he says, “All the nations surrounded me like bees around a honeycomb, and in the name of the Lord I drove them off” (Psalm 118:12). Do you see how he compares those who strike to a bee that stings, but compares the righteous to the bee that drips honey? For Scripture says, “The lips of righteous men drip wisdom” (Proverbs 10:31), and, “Good words are a honeycomb of honey, and their sweetness is healing for the soul” (Proverbs 16:24).

So, beloved, let us long for this sweetness of souls, I mean, with our whole soul. Let us fashion the spiritual honeycomb in the hidden workshop of the soul, and let us take the divine words as sweeter than honey and honeycomb. Much honey eaten often turns its sweetness to bitterness, ruins the stomach’s appetite, and overturns a person’s whole condition. But much of God’s word taken does not cloud the soul; it heals it, for its sweetness is healing for the soul. That wise author wanted to set out the difference between honey and the word, so he says, “Eating much honey is not good, but glorious words must be honored” (Proverbs 25:27).

Let us therefore keep always, beloved, the richly varied honeycomb, the divine and holy words. Just as a honeycomb is built from many different cells yet holds one good, so let divine Scripture be a honeycomb for us, composed from many different prophets yet dripping one honey of teaching. Such for us is also the honeycomb of the Fathers, fitted together from different generations yet dripping one grace and one spiritual teaching. But this is enough on these matters. By the prayers and intercessions of our common Father, may we increase the word by diligence, always carry out the divine law in our mind, and do what David spoke of, holding God’s law always in the midst of our belly, that is, the divine thoughts, so that we make it our rule to recognize the limits of nature, honor truth, despise the world, and send up glory to God, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
